interactive.title: Drag where i and j land
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in twelve small screens on one picture. A squared grid of the plane has its origin ringed and an F-shaped flag drawn on it. The F looks different in a mirror, so a flip shows at once. Two arrows start at the origin: i, one square across to (1, 0), and j, one square up to (0, 1). Their names sit in teal beside their tips. A faint copy of the starting grid stays behind. The rule is the mix of columns from What a matrix is. A matrix times (1, 0) takes 1 lot of column 1 and none of column 2, so i lands on column 1. In the same way j lands on column 2. Any point (x, y) is x lots of i plus y lots of j, so it lands on x lots of column 1 plus y lots of column 2. Every grid line and every corner of the flag is carried that way. Each step along a grid line adds the same arrow. Lines running across add column 1 at every step, and lines running up add column 2, so the lines stay straight, parallel and evenly spaced. The origin is no lots of anything, so it stays put. Beside the picture, or under it on a phone, the matrix is written large enough to read at 360 px, with i's landing spot down column 1 and j's down column 2. Dragging a tip snaps it to whole squares. The screens. 1, the matrix [2 −1; 1 1] played from the do-nothing grid: i slides to (2, 1) and the grid follows, with 1 × column 1 + 0 × column 2 written out. 2, a puzzle: where j lands under [2 −1; 1 1], with (−1, 1), (1, 1) and (2, 1) offered, j sliding there after Check. 3, the point (1, 2) tracked as a dot: it lands on 1 lot of (2, 1) plus 2 lots of (−1, 1), drawn nose to tail, which is (0, 3). 4, a puzzle: where (2, 1) lands under the same matrix, with (3, 3), (5, −1) and (4, 2) offered, the chain drawn only after Check. 5, both tips free to drag, and buttons Stretch [2 0; 0 3], Turn, Mirror [−1 0; 0 1], Shear [1 1; 0 1] and Squash, which wrap onto more lines on a narrow phone without splitting a word. Putting the tips back on (1, 0) and (0, 1) gives the do-nothing matrix [1 0; 0 1], and nothing moves. Its still is the mirror, read as: the mirror [−1 0; 0 1] sends i to (−1, 0) and leaves j, so the F faces the other way. 6, a puzzle from picture to matrix: the grid already moved, with i on (3, 1) and j on (0, 2), and [3 0; 1 2], [3 1; 0 2] and [0 3; 2 1] offered. 7, the turn: an angle slider from 0° to 360° in steps of 15°, opening at 30°. i's tip runs round the unit circle at (cos θ, sin θ), and j's tip stays a quarter turn ahead at (−sin θ, cos θ). The matrix reads [cos θ −sin θ; sin θ cos θ] with its values to two decimal places, [0.87 −0.5; 0.5 0.87] at 30°. Its still is 30°, read as: turned 30°, i lands on (0.87, 0.5) and j a quarter turn ahead on (−0.5, 0.87). 8, a puzzle from matrix to picture: which flag [0 −1; 1 0] makes, with the F turned a quarter anticlockwise, turned a quarter clockwise, and flipped over the line y = x offered, each as a small drawing with those words under it. 9, the squash [2 1; 4 2]: i lands on (2, 4) and j on (1, 2), both on one line through the origin, and the grid folds down onto that line with the flag as a short line. 10, a puzzle: which matrix squashes the plane onto a line, with [1 3; 2 6], [1 3; 6 2] and [3 0; 0 2] offered. 11, a mixed puzzle: where (2, 1) lands under the quarter turn [0 −1; 1 0], with (−1, 2), (1, −2) and (−2, 1) offered. 12, a mixed puzzle: which move no 2 by 2 matrix can make, with slide the flag 3 squares right, turn it a half turn, and mirror it in the up axis, the line x = 0, offered. The answer is the slide, because the origin is no lots of anything and stays put. Some screens show an idea and the rest ask you to try it. Each puzzle offers three answers, which wrap onto more lines on a narrow phone, and a wrong pick is drawn so you can see where it goes wrong.
interactive.ignores: The grid shows a small patch of the plane, which goes on for ever in every direction, and every point of it moves. Dragged tips snap to whole squares so the numbers stay easy, but a landing spot can be any point, as the turn's are. A slide of the whole plane can be done with a 3 by 3 matrix and an extra coordinate, which this picture does not show. A 3 by 3 matrix also moves space in the same way, with a third arrow k.

explain.text:
A 2 by 2 matrix can do more than hold two equations. It can move every point of the plane at once. Its two columns say where the arrows i and j land, and every other point follows from those two.

Remember the mix of columns? A matrix times a column of amounts is x lots of column 1 plus y lots of column 2. The arrow i is (1, 0), one square across. So the matrix times i is 1 lot of column 1 and none of column 2. That is column 1 itself. In the same way j is (0, 1), so it lands on column 2. The matrix sends i and j to its own columns.[^1]

Every other point is built from i and j. The point (x, y) is x lots of i plus y lots of j. So it lands on x lots of column 1 plus y lots of column 2.[^2] Take [2 −1; 1 1]. Here i lands on (2, 1) and j lands on (−1, 1). The point (1, 2) lands on 1 lot of (2, 1) plus 2 lots of (−1, 1), which is (0, 3). Each step along a grid line adds the same arrow. Lines running across add column 1 at every step, and lines running up add column 2. So the grid lines stay straight, parallel and evenly spaced. The origin is no lots of anything, so it never moves. A move of the whole plane like this is called a [[transformation]]. Four numbers describe it completely, because they are just two landing spots. Write the landing spots across as rows instead, and you get a different move. [2 1; −1 1] sends i to (2, −1), not (2, 1).

Named moves have named landing spots. A stretch keeps i and j on their axes but longer, as [2 0; 0 3] does. A mirror such as [−1 0; 0 1] sends i to (−1, 0) and keeps j, so the F faces the other way. A [[shear]] keeps i and slides j along to (1, 1), so the squares lean like a pushed stack of paper. A turn anticlockwise through θ sends i to (cos θ, sin θ), the tip of the arm on the unit circle. A quarter turn anticlockwise sends an arrow's across part up and its up part to the left, so (a, b) becomes (−b, a). j starts a quarter turn ahead of i, so it lands on (−sin θ, cos θ). If both landing spots fall on one line through the origin, every mix of them does too, and the whole plane is squashed flat onto that line.

**A 2 by 2 matrix moves the whole plane, and its two columns are where i and j land.**[^1]

analogy.text: Think of marking out fixings on a board by measuring from one corner. Each mark is so many steps along one tape and so many steps up another. Lay the two tapes at a slant, or use a tape with longer steps, and every mark you set out moves with them. Where each tape's first step ends is all you need to find every mark.
analogy.breaks: Real tapes share one step size, and you lay them square on purpose. A matrix can give a step that points backwards, which turns the board over. It can also lay both tapes along one line, which squashes the board flat.

practice.text:
- Follow i: find where (1, 0) lands. Write it down column 1.
- Follow j: find where (0, 1) lands. Write it down column 2.
- To move any point (x, y), take x lots of column 1 plus y lots of column 2.
- Check one easy point by drawing it.

**Rule of thumb:** Columns are landing spots, and i's comes first.

**Worked example:** A quarter turn anticlockwise sends i to (0, 1) and j to (−1, 0). So its matrix is [0 −1; 1 0]. The point (3, 2) lands on 3 lots of (0, 1) plus 2 lots of (−1, 0), which is (−2, 3). Check by turning it in your head. A point 3 across and 2 up, turned a quarter, ends 3 up and 2 to the left.

**The turn anticlockwise through θ** is [cos θ −sin θ; sin θ cos θ]. To check the minus is in the right corner, put θ = 90°. That gives [0 −1; 1 0], which sends i straight up.

**Common mistakes**
- Writing a landing spot across a row. [2 1; −1 1] sends i to (2, −1), not (2, 1).
- Putting i's landing spot in column 2.
- Putting the turn's minus in the wrong corner. [0 1; −1 0] turns clockwise.
- Expecting a matrix to slide a shape. The origin is no lots of anything, so it never moves.
